text: Good evening. I am calling to order the HRTD committee meeting for the month of April. It is April 27th. Joined with me today are Mr. John Beatty and Mr. Jeff Morse. Do we have anyone signed up for public comment?

Okay, so we try to have providers throughout the county. When you're dealing with workers' compensation, there are specific practices that have to be followed, et cetera. So we work with our third-party administrator to develop the list of physicians that are the initial contact for an employee so that we can make sure that they're getting the care that we want to make sure they're getting the care that they need to get.

So it depends. If it's as simple as taking out stitches, probably. If they're being referred to an orthopedist, our provider works with them to find an orthopedist that's on their list of approved providers that's close to their home address.

Okay, thank you so much. I don't have any further questions. Mr. Morris? Thank you. I do want to go back to the attending physician. This is specific to workers' comp. We have health care program at Cigna, I'm sorry, that provides health care wherever our employees are, whether they be across the country, on a trip, or anywhere else.

So they can be seen by any of those. This is specific to workers' comp claims, correct? That's correct. And so when you say the injured or ill employee must be attended by a physician on the approved list, that's not for ongoing care. That is for confirmation that they're eligible for workers' comp?

Is that? Well, yes and no. So an employee who's injured and the claim is approved by the third-party administrator as a valid claim, then the employee is going to continue to care with a health care provider under the workers' compensation program.

So whether it's an orthopedist that is approved or a, I don't know, I'm trying to think what other ones we have, primarily the orthopedist neurologist, if we have somebody with a head injury, If someone, that's a lifetime benefit, medical benefit for that injury.

If someone leaves the area and they need to seek care, then PMA will work with them to identify a provider in the area that they're currently residing in. Okay, so would they also work with them to provide care for, if they, suppose they did live in West Virginia, a care from a physician in West Virginia as well?

If there was a physician in West Virginia that is on the approved provider list, yes. And there are some, most of them are in Virginia because it's Virginia workers' compensation. That's correct. But we do try to make sure that they have a minimal amount or as close as possible. We also pay mileage. So if they're going to see a provider, if they're going to a physical therapist, if they're doing a work hardening program, we pay mileage for all of those.
Is this common for neighboring counties? Do they do their workers' comp the same way? Yes. Thank you.

And just, sorry, one more follow-up question on that. Is that a requirement of our insurance, or is it more so just the general practice and how that runs? Again, I'm thinking not so much the cost of the travel, but if you require physical therapy and you're in pain and not having to drive yourself to your appointment, the closer your appointment, the better for yourself and your comfort as you're trying to handle your injury.

So I do not believe it is required that they be providers in this state, but we have more negotiating power with providers in this state. The TPA has more negotiating power with providers in the state.

If we have somebody who is further out and it is not practicable for them to get to a care provider, then PMA would work with them. But generally speaking, yes, they're going to be in Virginia. It's Virginia Workers' Comp. And so that's kind of the guidelines that we operate under.

Okay. I would say if there is a practice where we have been able to work with people to find a kind of off-list provider in the past, that that should be something that we should be upfront about in the policy. Okay.
